clue.text: Author of The Broken Road and The Master Builder?

definitions.meaning: A. E. W. ... wrote the 1907 novel The Broken Road
a skilled stoneworker is a builder par excellence, with a nod to Ibsen's play title

explanation.surface: A quiz question asking who wrote two books, one of them Ibsen's play.
explanation.walkthrough: The Master Builder looks like a second literary title, but here it is a description of the tradesman who works in stone.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist A. E. W. Mason wrote The Broken Road; a stoneworking craftsman is a builder.

clue.text: Called up three sections of military bodies perhaps

definitions.text: Called up three sections of military bodies perhaps

parts.words: Called up three sections of military bodies perhaps
parts.note: call-up of army, navy and air force at once, three branches of the armed services put on a war footing

explanation.surface: Several units of the armed forces have been summoned for service.
explanation.definitionFit: Troops summoned to active service in wartime have been called up, put on a war footing.

clue.text: Sergeant went swiftly back in two directions

indicators.note: the word in tells us one piece sits inside the pair of compass points

parts.note: S and E are the compass points south and east

indicators.note: back tells us the past-tense verb for running is read in reverse order

parts.note: went swiftly means ran

explanation.surface: A sergeant hurried back, darting first one way and then another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns RAN into NAR, which goes 'in' S and E. Snare is one of the two sergeants (with Fang) in Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 2.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare names one of the officers sent to arrest Falstaff Snare; he is a sergeant in Henry IV Part 2.

clue.text: "In Heaven, / Where honour due and reverence none (Paradise Lost)

definitions.text: "In Heaven, / Where honour due and reverence none (Paradise Lost)

parts.words: "In Heaven, / Where honour due and reverence none (Paradise Lost)
parts.note: a quotation from Milton's epic with its final word left out, to be supplied by the solver

explanation.surface: A line from Milton's Paradise Lost with its last word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's line ends with the verb meaning fails to pay attention to, completing 'reverence none ...'.

clue.text: Roth's description of emancipation?

parts.note: a Philip Roth novel title read literally as a phrase for setting someone free

explanation.surface: A question about how the novelist Philip Roth might describe liberation.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Roth's 1962 novel has this title, and releasing one's hold on someone is a way of freeing them.

clue.text: Issue of Homer turning up in basilica

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up means the letters are read from bottom to top
in tells us the letters sit inside the word basilica

explanation.surface: Homer's offspring appear upside down in a great church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Homer' suggests the Greek poet, but it is Homer Simpson; 'in' picks ASIL from basilica and 'turning up' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Simpsons, Homer's elder daughter has this name, so she is his issue, his child.

clue.text: Constable's article on film star Will and author John

parts.note: the definite article
Will Hay was a British comic film actor of the 1930s
John Wain was an English novelist and poet

explanation.surface: A painter's work featuring a film comedian and a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constable's' means a work by John Constable, the English landscape painter; 'on' simply joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: John Constable's most famous painting, an 1821 landscape of a cart in a Suffolk river, bears this title.

clue.text: Islands featuring in endless game

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: endless means the board game loses its final letter

parts.note: chess is a board game

explanation.surface: Some islands are the scene of an interminable match.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scotland an 'inch' is a small island, as in Inchcolm; 'endless' cuts the last S from CHESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Inch is a Scottish word for a small island, found in many place names.

clue.text: What peepers have in in the long grass, according to Sitwell

definitions.text: What peepers have in in the long grass, according to Sitwell

parts.words: What peepers have in in the long grass, according to Sitwell
parts.note: Edith Sitwell's poem Long Steel Grass in Façade speaks of a Spanish woman's boastful eyes

explanation.surface: A question about what eyes possess in tall grass, citing the poet Sitwell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the long grass' is the poem Long Steel Grass from Façade, which has the line 'Her eyes' gasconade'; 'peepers' are eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sitwell's poem gives eyes a swaggering boastfulness, which is what this word for bravado means.

clue.text: Crime drama in which you'll see a wizard, a queen and king

parts.note: the Wizard of Oz
R for regina, Latin for queen
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A TV thriller featuring a wizard and royalty.
explanation.definitionFit: This Netflix series about money laundering in Missouri is a crime drama.

clue.text: Wren's construction, a gracious signal to the French

definitions.meaning: P. C. Wren wrote the 1924 Foreign Legion novel with this title

definitions.text: a gracious signal to the French
definitions.meaning: French for a fine gesture, a noble or generous act

explanation.surface: A building by the architect Wren, and a polite gesture made towards France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wren' suggests the architect Christopher Wren, but it is the novelist P. C. Wren.
explanation.definitionFit: P. C. Wren's novel has this title, and in French the phrase means a fine gesture.

clue.text: One seen in epic as Caesar-killer

indicators.note: seen in tells us the letters are found running through the words epic as Caesar

explanation.surface: A character appears in a classical tale as the murderer of Julius Caesar.
explanation.definitionFit: Casca was the first conspirator to stab Julius Caesar, so he was one of his assassins.

clue.text: Compositions performed by first violin to audience?

indicators.note: to audience tells us we want what a listener hears, not the spelling

parts.note: the first violin of an orchestra is its leader

explanation.surface: Musical pieces played by the principal violinist for listeners.
explanation.walkthrough: The orchestra's first violin is called the leader; 'to audience' says it is heard, giving the German word for songs.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieder are German art songs, such as those by Schubert, so they are musical compositions.

clue.text: Get hair hidden under this?

parts.note: get means have, as in get or have a cold
a lock is a tress of hair

explanation.surface: A question about what to wear to keep your hair covered.
explanation.walkthrough: A havelock is a cloth cover on a cap hanging down to protect the neck, so hair is hidden under it.
explanation.definitionFit: This cap cover, named after General Henry Havelock, hangs over the neck and hides the hair beneath.

clue.text: A Constable, good chap, one, say, turning up to arrest woman

indicators.note: to arrest means the other pieces hold the woman captive inside them

parts.note: ST, saint, is a good person
taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up means the abbreviation for say is read upwards

parts.note: say means for example, EG
hen is slang for a woman

explanation.surface: A policeman, a gentleman and others rise to detain a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A Constable' is a painting by John Constable, not a police officer. 'turning up' reverses EG, and 'to arrest' means the woman ends up held among the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: John Constable painted a celebrated watercolour of the Wiltshire stone circle, so it is one of his works.

clue.text: Ramshackle place in which compose sea songs?

definitions.meaning: a settlement of crude huts on the edge of a city
read literally, a town for making sailors' work songs

explanation.surface: A rundown settlement where people write sea songs.
explanation.definitionFit: A district of improvised huts is a ramshackle settlement; read literally it is a town for sea songs.

clue.text: God-like angels lie about

indicators.note: about signals the letters of angels lie are moved around

explanation.surface: Divine angels tell untruths here and there.
explanation.definitionFit: Omniscience, seeing everything, is an attribute of a deity.

clue.text: Enthusiast has Gainsborough initially, then Sergeant

parts.note: an enthusiast is a fan

indicators.note: initially means we take only the opening letter of Gainsborough

explanation.surface: An admirer owns a Gainsborough and then a portrait by Sargent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gainsborough' and 'Sergeant' (sounding like the painter Sargent) suggest art; Fang is a sergeant in Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 2.
explanation.definitionFit: Fang is one of the officers sent to arrest Falstaff in Henry IV Part 2, a sergeant.

clue.text: G&S including strange crooked peaky blinders

indicators.note: including means the operetta pair holds the reworked word inside

parts.note: G and S stand for Gilbert and Sullivan

indicators.note: crooked signals the letters of strange are bent out of order

explanation.surface: Gilbert and Sullivan include some odd, dishonest criminals.
explanation.walkthrough: The Peaky Blinders were a Birmingham street gang, made famous by a TV drama.
explanation.definitionFit: The Peaky Blinders were a criminal gang, so its members were organised criminals.

clue.text: Constable's to track one of Yates's company

parts.note: to track someone is to dog them
Dornford Yates wrote the Berry and Co. stories

explanation.surface: A painter goes after a member of a writer's circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constable' suggests the painter, but Dogberry is the bumbling constable in Much Ado About Nothing; 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogberry is the comic officer of the watch in Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing.

clue.text: Constable left to succeed retired judge

indicators.note: to succeed means the abbreviation comes after the reversed piece
retired means withdrawn, so the word for judge is read backwards

parts.note: lud is the address to a judge, as in m'lud

explanation.surface: A policeman departed to take over from a judge who had stepped down.
explanation.walkthrough: Dull is the constable in Love's Labour's Lost; 'retired' reverses LUD to DUL.
explanation.definitionFit: Dull is the slow-witted officer of the law in Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost.

clue.text: "A kind of—— lumber-room, full of old chairs and tables, upside down" (Bleak House)

definitions.text: "A kind of—— lumber-room, full of old chairs and tables, upside down" (Bleak House)

parts.words: "A kind of—— lumber-room, full of old chairs and tables, upside down" (Bleak House)
parts.note: a Dickens quotation with a gap for an adjective meaning from the opposite side of the world

explanation.surface: A quotation from Dickens describing a topsy-turvy junk room.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things from the far side of the globe, where people stand upside down.

clue.text: Girl, one occupying topsyturvy cabin

indicators.note: occupying means one piece takes up residence inside another
topsyturvy signals the letters of cabin are jumbled

parts.note: a means one

explanation.surface: A girl and a companion live in a disordered hut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topsyturvy' jumbles CABIN into BINC, and 'occupying' puts A inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Bianca is a female first name, as in Shakespeare's Taming of the Shrew.

clue.text: Reportedly first person to refer to vision

indicators.note: reportedly tells us we want words as heard, not as spelt

parts.note: the first person is I, and to refer to is to cite

explanation.surface: Apparently, the earliest person to mention sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I cite' said aloud sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The faculty of seeing is sight or vision.

clue.text: Constable to quiver about losing book

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the shaken word is read backwards
losing means one letter is dropped from the word for quiver

parts.note: to quiver is to wobble

explanation.surface: A policeman shakes, without his book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' drops one B from WOBBLE to get WOBLE, and 'about' reverses it; Elbow is the constable in Measure for Measure.
explanation.definitionFit: Elbow is the simple officer of the law in Shakespeare's Measure for Measure.

clue.text: Sparky religious leader seen in railwayjunction

definitions.text: Sparky religious leader seen in railwayjunction

parts.words: Sparky religious leader seen in railwayjunction
parts.note: a Muriel Spark title about a convent head at Crewe, the famous English rail junction

explanation.surface: A lively churchwoman spotted at a railway junction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sparky' means of Muriel Spark: her novel is The Abbess of Crewe, and Crewe is a famous railway junction town in Cheshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of a community of nuns is a female religious superior.

clue.text: Holmes's sister, climbing solo

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: solo means alone

explanation.surface: Sherlock's sibling goes rock-climbing by herself.
explanation.definitionFit: Nancy Springer's novels and the Netflix films give Sherlock a younger sibling with this name.

clue.text: Burly actor-singer

parts.note: Burl plus the surname ... the American folk singer and film actor; the y is a hint to split the name

explanation.definitionFit: Burl Ives was an American folk singer and Oscar-winning actor.

clue.text: Prolific symphonist with a life in films

definitions.meaning: Monty Python's Life of ... is a 1979 film comedy

explanation.surface: A composer who has also had a career in the cinema.
explanation.definitionFit: Havergal Brian composed many symphonies; the Monty Python film is Life of Brian.

clue.text: Ravenous exclamation not to be repeated

definitions.meaning: the cry of the bird in Poe's poem The Raven

explanation.surface: A hungry cry that won't be heard again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ravenous' looks like hungry, but means of Poe's Raven, whose refrain is this word.
explanation.definitionFit: Poe's raven repeats this word, which also means at no time again.

clue.text: Headgear suppliers having dodgy ski wager about end of slalom

indicators.note: about means the jumbled letters go around the last letter of the race
dodgy signals the letters of ski wager are unreliable and rearranged
end of means take just the final letter of slalom

explanation.surface: Hat makers placing a risky bet on a skiing race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dodgy' jumbles SKI WAGER, and 'about' puts it round M.
explanation.definitionFit: People who make periwigs supply a kind of head covering.

clue.text: How long it took Virginia to write?

definitions.text: How long it took Virginia to write?

parts.words: How long it took Virginia to write?
parts.note: a span of time, also the title of a Virginia Woolf novel of 1937

explanation.surface: A question about how much time Virginia Woolf spent writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Virginia Woolf wrote The Years; long periods of time are measured in twelve-month spans.
